citations.quote: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim: By openness choose $R>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,2R)\subset U$. Continuity of $X$ and $DX$ at $q_0$ gives finite $M,L\ge0$ bounding $\|X\|$ on $\overline B(q_0,R)$ and $\|DX\|$ on $B(q_0,2R)$. By [F1] $X$ is totally differentiable there, and [F2] applied to the convex ball $B(q_0,2R)$ gives $\|X(u)-X(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|$ for $u,v\in\overline B(q_0,R)$.

Let $\mathcal C$ be the closed ball in $C([-\delta,\delta],\mathbb R^m)$ of curves with values in $\overline B(q_0,R)$, with the supremum norm. It is complete: a Cauchy sequence converges uniformly componentwise because $\mathbb R^m$ is complete; its uniform limit is continuous and remains in the closed ball. For $p\in\overline B(q_0,R/2)$ define $T_p\gamma(t):=p+\int_0^t X(\gamma(s))\,ds$. The integrand is continuous and hence integrable by [F3]. Choose $\delta>0$ with $M\delta\le R/2$ and $L\delta<1$. Then $T_p$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself, since $\|T_p\gamma(t)-q_0\|\le\|p-q_0\|+M|t|\le R$, and is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta$.

Starting at the constant curve $\gamma_0(t)=p$, iterate $\gamma_{k+1}=T_p\gamma_k$. If $\kappa=L\delta<1$, then $\|\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_k\|_\infty\le\kappa^k\|\gamma_1-\gamma_0\|_\infty$; the geometric tail bound makes $(\gamma_k)$ uniformly Cauchy. Its limit $\phi(\cdot,p)\in\mathcal C$ is a fixed point by the contraction bound. Any two fixed points have distance at most $\kappa$ times that distance, so they coincide.

For $g(s)=X(\phi(s,p))$, continuity and [F3] make every component Riemann integrable. At an interior $t$, the difference quotient of $\phi(t,p)=p+\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$ differs from $g(t)$ by at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|g(s)-g(t)\|$, which tends to zero by continuity; thus $\partial_t\phi=X(\phi)$. Conversely any $C^1$ solution staying in the ball satisfies the fixed-point equation by [F4], so uniqueness of the fixed point is uniqueness of the IVP.

If $p,p'$ lie in $\overline B(q_0,R/2)$, subtract their fixed-point equations and take suprema to obtain $\|\phi(\cdot,p)-\phi(\cdot,p')\|_\infty\le\|p-p'\|+L\delta\|\phi(\cdot,p)-\phi(\cdot,p')\|_\infty$. Since $L\delta<1$, division gives the local Lipschitz estimate $(1-L\delta)^{-1}\|p-p'\|$.

Whenever the compositions remain in the chosen ball, both $t\mapsto\phi(t+s,p)$ and $t\mapsto\phi(t,\phi(s,p))$ solve the same IVP at $t=0$, with initial value $\phi(s,p)$. Uniqueness from step 3.1 gives the local flow law; setting $t=-s$ gives the local inverse relation.

citations.quote: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

derivations.claim:
For $p$ near $q$ put $\Delta_h(t):=\phi_X^t(p+h)-\phi_X^t(p)$. The integral equations from [F1] and the one-variable fundamental theorem applied to $\theta\mapsto X(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))$ give
$$\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_0^t A_h(s)\Delta_h(s)\,ds,\quad A_h(s):=\int_0^1DX(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))\,d\theta.$$
The segments lie in $K$ after shrinking the initial ball and time interval. The local Lipschitz estimate in [F1] gives $\sup_t\|\Delta_h(t)\|=O(\|h\|)$. Uniform continuity of $DX$ on $K$ from [F4] makes $A_h(s)$ converge uniformly to $DX(\phi_X^s(p))$ as $h\to0$.

The linear integral equation $J(t)=I+\int_0^tDX(\phi_X^s(p))J(s)\,ds$ has a unique continuous solution by the same complete-curve-space contraction argument as [F1], after retaining $L\delta<1$. Subtracting $J(t)h$ from the equation in step 1.1 gives a remainder $R_h$ satisfying $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+\delta\|A_h-DX(\phi_X^s(p))\|_\infty\|\Delta_h\|_\infty=o(\|h\|)$. Hence $D_q\phi_X^t(p)=J(t,p)$. The continuous integrand in the equation for $J$ has average over $[t,t+h]$ tending to its value at $t$: the quotient error is at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|DX(\phi_X^s(p))J(s,p)-DX(\phi_X^t(p))J(t,p)\|$, which tends to zero. Thus $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(p))J$ and $J(0,p)=I$.

Write $J_h(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p+h)$ and $J_0(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p)$. Subtracting their integral equations gives
$$J_h-J_0=\int_0^t DX(\phi_h)(J_h-J_0)\,ds+\int_0^t(DX(\phi_h)-DX(\phi_0))J_0\,ds,$$
where $\phi_h=\phi_X^s(p+h)$ and $\phi_0=\phi_X^s(p)$. Boundedness of $D^2X$ on $K$ and $\phi_h-\phi_0=O(\|h\|)$ bound the second integral by $C\|h\|$ for a fixed $C$; the first integral has norm at most $L\delta\|J_h-J_0\|_\infty$. Since $L\delta<1$, absorption gives $J_h-J_0=O(\|h\|)$ uniformly in time. Uniform continuity of $D^2X$ on $K$ and the integral mean-value formula give, uniformly in $s$,
$$DX(\phi_h)-DX(\phi_0)=D^2X(\phi_0)[\phi_h-\phi_0,\cdot]+o(\|h\|)
=D^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,\cdot]+o(\|h\|),$$
using $\phi_h-\phi_0=J_0h+o(\|h\|)$ from step 1.2. Also $J_h=J_0+O(\|h\|)$. Substitute these expansions in the subtracted equation: the forcing term is
$$\int_0^tD^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,J_0(\cdot)]\,ds+o(\|h\|),$$
uniformly in time. For each $h$, let $K_h$ solve the linear integral equation obtained by retaining this displayed leading term and the coefficient $DX(\phi_0)$; existence and uniqueness follow from the same contraction bound $L\delta<1$. Then $R_h:=J_h-J_0-K_h$ satisfies $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+o(\|h\|)$, so $R_h=o(\|h\|)$. Thus $D_pJ[h](v)=K_h(v)$, and, writing $K_2[u,v]=D_q^2\phi_X[u,v]$, it is the unique solution
$$K_2(t)[u,v]=\int_0^t\big(DX(\phi_X^s)K_2(s)[u,v]+D^2X(\phi_X^s)[J(s)u,J(s)v]\big)\,ds.$$
The integral equation makes $K_2$ bilinear in $(u,v)$; the same contraction estimate and continuity of its coefficients give continuous dependence on $(t,p)$.

Since $\partial_t\phi_X=X(\phi_X)$, the chain rule [F2] and the established continuous first and second derivatives in $q$ give continuous mixed time derivatives; differentiating once more in $t$ gives $\partial_t^2\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)X(\phi_X)$. Hence the local flow is jointly $C^2$.

Let $V(t):=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and $W(t):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)$. By [F2] and the variational equation, $V'=DY(\phi_X^t)X(\phi_X^t)$ and $W'=DX(\phi_X^t)W$. The identity $[X,Y]=0$ makes $V$ solve this same linear equation with $V(0)=W(0)=Y(q)$; uniqueness from the contraction argument gives $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$.

For fixed $t$, the curve $s\mapsto\phi_X^t(\phi_Y^s(q))$ has derivative $D\phi_X^t\,Y(\phi_Y^s(q))=Y(\phi_X^t(\phi_Y^s(q))$ by step 3.1, and starts at $\phi_X^t(q)$. It is therefore the $Y$-flow from that initial point; IVP uniqueness from [F1] yields $\phi_X^t\phi_Y^s(q)=\phi_Y^s\phi_X^t(q)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, $n\ge1$, with coordinates $(x_1,\ldots,x_n,z)$. A $C^2$ one-form on $U$ is a field of linear functionals on tangent vectors of the form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(x,z)\,dx_i+b(x,z)\,dz$, where every coefficient is twice continuously differentiable. At $q\in U$, it acts by $\omega_q(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)=\sum_i a_i(q)u_i+b(q)w$. It is nonsingular on $U$ when $\omega_q\ne0$ for every $q$; then $H_q:=\ker\omega_q$ is an $n$-dimensional subspace of $T_qU\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$.

For one-forms $\alpha,\beta$, their exterior product is the alternating two-form $(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u)$. For a one-form $\alpha$ and a two-form $\sigma$, $(\alpha\wedge\sigma)(u,v,w)=\alpha(u)\sigma(v,w)-\alpha(v)\sigma(u,w)+\alpha(w)\sigma(u,v)$. The exterior derivative of the displayed $C^2$ form is the $C^1$ two-form

$$d\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dx_j+\sum_{i=1}^n(\partial_i b-\partial_z a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dz.$$

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

On a neighborhood $W$, an integrating factor for $\omega$ is a nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ for which $\mu\omega=dS$ for some $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS$ nowhere zero. This definition is local; it asserts neither a global potential on $U$ nor a physical identification or calibration of $S$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim:
Fix $q\in U$ and distinct coordinates $i,j$. Choose $h,k>0$ small enough that the coordinate rectangle from $q$ to $q+he_i+ke_j$ lies in $U$, and set $\Delta=S(q+he_i+ke_j)-S(q+he_i)-S(q+ke_j)+S(q)$. By [F4] the second partials are uniformly continuous on the chosen closed rectangle. Applying [F2] to coordinate segments and [F3] to their continuous derivatives, Newton–Leibniz gives
$$\Delta=\int_0^h\!\int_0^k S_{ij}(q+se_i+te_j)\,dt\,ds=\int_0^k\!\int_0^h S_{ji}(q+se_i+te_j)\,ds\,dt.$$
Each equality follows by taking the two endpoint differences in the outer coordinate and then applying Newton–Leibniz to the inner difference; both integrands are continuous by $S\in C^2$.

Divide both expressions in step 1.1 by $hk$ and let $h,k\downarrow0$. Continuity of $S_{ij}$ and $S_{ji}$ makes each average tend to its value at $q$, so $S_{ij}(q)=S_{ji}(q)$. Since $q,i,j$ were arbitrary, the coordinate formula in [F1] gives $d(dS)=0$.

Put $\lambda:=1/\mu\in C^1(U)$. Then $\omega=\lambda dS$. Expanding the coordinate derivative by the product rule and using step 1.2 yields $d\omega=d\lambda\wedge dS$. Therefore $\omega\wedge d\omega=\lambda\,dS\wedge d\lambda\wedge dS=0$, because the alternating product vanishes when the same one-form $dS$ occurs twice.

U is open, so no boundary-point extension is claimed; the rectangle argument is restricted to rectangles in U, step 1.1.

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim: Let $D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ and $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ with $P(x,y)=-y/(x^2+y^2)$ and $Q(x,y)=x/(x^2+y^2)$. The domain $D$ is open since each nonzero point has a ball avoiding the origin, and the coefficients are smooth with $(P,Q)\ne(0,0)$ at every point. It is path-connected: if the segment joining $p,q\in D$ avoids $0$, use that segment; if it contains $0$, then $p,q,0$ are collinear, and a nonzero vector $r$ perpendicular to $p$ makes both segments $[p,r]$ and $[r,q]$ avoid $0$.
Writing $r^2=x^2+y^2$, direct differentiation gives $\partial_xQ=(y^2-x^2)/r^4=\partial_yP$, so $d\omega=(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)dx\wedge dy=0$ on $D$.

The unit circle $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, $0\le t\le2\pi$, lies in $D$ and is closed. Along it $(P,Q)=(-\sin t,\cos t)=\gamma'(t)$, hence [F2] gives $\int_\gamma\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi$ by [F4].

If $\omega=dS$ globally on $D$, then $F=\nabla S$ for the corresponding vector field, and [F3] would give $\int_\gamma\omega=S(\gamma(2\pi))-S(\gamma(0))=0$, contradicting step 2.1. Thus $\omega$ is closed but not globally exact. This does not assert that every possible global integrating factor is absent.
